    Advisor for vegan: ordination and multivariate tests

    Source: R/advisor-vegan.R
    vegan-advisor.Rd

    Built-in advisor for the vegan package, for community data in the wide format vegan uses (one row per site, one column per species).

    • Before (question = "vegan"): reports the number of sites and species, the share of zeros, and the length of the main gradient. From these it recommends a linear or a unimodal method, NMDS for an unconstrained view, and PERMANOVA (vegan::adonis2()) with its companion check of dispersion (vegan::betadisper()).

    The gradient-length rule. The gradient length is the length of the longest axis of a detrended correspondence analysis (vegan::decorana(), detrending by segments, on log(y + 1) abundances or presence-absence), in standard-deviation (SD) units of species turnover. This is the value CANOCO reports. Over about 4 SD the species composition turns over completely.

    Gradient lengthSpecies responsesMethod
    below 3 SDmostly monotoniclinear: PCA, RDA (on Hellinger-transformed abundances)
    3 to 4 SDmixedboth appropriate; tidyvisor gives RDA, with CCA as the alternative
    above 4 SDunimodal (rise and fall)unimodal: CA, CCA

    The rule guides; it does not decide. Hellinger-transformed RDA (Legendre & Gallagher 2001) and distance-based methods (NMDS, db-RDA, PERMANOVA) are valid at any gradient length.

    • After: explains vegan::metaMDS() (stress against Clarke's benchmarks), vegan::rda(), vegan::cca(), vegan::capscale() and vegan::dbrda() (variance explained, adjusted R-squared, permutation tests), vegan::adonis2() and anova() tables, vegan::betadisper() and vegan::envfit().

    For long-format data, tidydiversity offers the same analyses through ord_fit(); its advisor answers tidyvisor(data, abundance = ...).

    Usage

    tv_advise_vegan(
  x,
  question = "vegan",
  species = NULL,
  env = NULL,
  blocks = NULL,
  time = NULL,
  lon = NULL,
  lat = NULL,
  traits = NULL,
  ...
)

tv_interpret_vegan(x, permutations = 999, ...)

    Arguments

    x

    A wide data frame of sites (advice), or a vegan result (interpretation).

    question

    The question; set by advise().

    species

    Names of the species columns (default: every numeric column not in env).

    env

    Names of the explanatory columns, if any.

    blocks

    Name of a column of blocks: permutations are restricted to within blocks (tidydiversity::ord_design()).

    time

    Name of a time (or transect position) column: permutations keep the order of the series.

    lon, lat

    Names of coordinate columns: the advice adds variation partitioning between environment and space (tidymapr::geo_varpart()).

    traits

    Name of a trait table, if traits were measured: the advice adds trait-environment analysis (dc-CA or RLQ).

    ...

    Ignored.

    permutations

    Number of permutations for the tests run while interpreting a constrained ordination.

    Value

    A tv_advice or a tv_interpretation object.

    References

    Anderson, M.J. (2001). A new method for non-parametric multivariate analysis of variance. Austral Ecology 26, 32-46.

    Clarke, K.R. (1993). Non-parametric multivariate analyses of changes in community structure. Australian Journal of Ecology 18, 117-143.

    Leps, J. & Smilauer, P. (2003). Multivariate Analysis of Ecological Data using CANOCO. Cambridge University Press. (Second edition for Canoco 5, 2014.)

    Legendre, P. & Gallagher, E.D. (2001). Ecologically meaningful transformations for ordination of species data. Oecologia 129, 271-280.

    Ter Braak, C.J.F. & Smilauer, P. (2012). Canoco Reference Manual and User's Guide: Software for Ordination (version 5.0). Microcomputer Power, Ithaca.

    Examples

    data("dune", "dune.env", package = "vegan")
tidyvisor(cbind(dune, dune.env), question = "vegan", env = c("A1", "Management"))
#> 
#> ── tidyvisor: which analysis? ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Question: vegan
#> 
#> ── What the data show ──
#> 
#> • Sites: 20
#> • Species: 30
#> • Zeros: 67% — many zeros: avoid Euclidean distances on raw counts (double-zero
#>   problem); use Hellinger or Bray-Curtis
#> • Gradient length (longest DCA axis, SD units): 3.52 — between 3 and 4 SD:
#>   intermediate; linear and unimodal methods are both appropriate
#> 
#> ── Recommended ──
#> 
#> Model: Redundancy analysis (RDA) on Hellinger-transformed abundances
#> Branch: constrained ordination (a picture of the gradients your variables
#> explain, tested by permutation). With a gradient of 3 to 4 SD, linear and
#> unimodal methods are both appropriate; CCA (vegan::cca(comm ~ ...)) is the
#> alternative. The Hellinger transformation removes the double-zero problem so
#> RDA can be used on community data (Legendre & Gallagher 2001).
#> comm <- data[species]
#> m <- vegan::rda(vegan::decostand(comm, "hellinger") ~ A1 + Management, data = data)
#> Test: Permutation tests of the model, the axes and each term
#> Community data are not multivariate normal; permutations give valid p-values.
#> anova(m); anova(m, by = "terms"); vegan::RsquareAdj(m)
#> Alternative: PERMANOVA on Bray-Curtis dissimilarities
#> Branch: multivariate test (a p-value, no picture). Tests differences in
#> composition without assuming a linear or unimodal response (Anderson 2001).
#> vegan::adonis2(comm ~ A1 + Management, data = data, method = "bray", by = "terms")
#> Check: Compare the dispersion of the Management groups
#> PERMANOVA is sensitive to differences in spread as well as location; a
#> significant betadisper test means a PERMANOVA difference may reflect spread.
#> b <- vegan::betadisper(vegan::vegdist(comm), data$Management); anova(b)
#> Groups: To find the species combinations that best separate the Management
#> groups: canonical variate analysis
#> CVA (discriminant analysis) maximises the separation between predefined groups;
#> it needs fewer species than sites, so use a few species or the first PCA axes.
#> tidydiversity::ord_cva(data, abundance = abundance, group = "Management")
#> Interpret: Plain-language explanation of the result
#> Variance explained, tests and how to read the plot.
#> tidyvisor(m)
m <- vegan::rda(vegan::decostand(dune, "hellinger") ~ A1 + Management, dune.env)
tidyvisor(m, permutations = 99)
#> 
#> ── tidyvisor: what the results show ────────────────────────────────────────────
#> 
#> ── Overview ──
#> 
#> • Redundancy analysis (RDA) of 20 sites with 4 constraining degrees of freedom.
#> 
#> ── Fit ──
#> 
#> • The explanatory variables account for 38.6% of the total variance (adjusted
#>   R-squared 22.2%, corrected for the number of variables).
#> • The first constrained axis shows 17.5% of the total.
#> 
#> ── Tests ──
#> 
#> • Whole model: F = 2.35, p = 0.010 (99 permutations).
#> • A1 explains 13.0% of the variation: F = 3.17, p = 0.010.
#> • Management explains 25.6% of the variation: F = 2.08, p = 0.010.
#> 
#> ── Reading the plot ──
#> 
#> • In an RDA triplot, the angle between arrows approximates correlation; project
#>   sites or species onto an arrow to read their relation to it.
#> • Look at the axes' explained variance before reading patterns along them.
